name: Bending stress
seoDesc: Bending stress: work out inner depth (di) from the distance to surface and the area moment of inertia (Iₓ). A free construction calculator with the…
summary: Supply the distance to surface, the area moment of inertia (Iₓ) and the x-axis to bottom surface and the Bending stress calculator solves for inner depth (di). That makes it useful for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Bending stress calculator work?
sections.html:
The Bending stress calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports inner depth (di) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the cross-section of the beam); then you type in the distance to surface (yc), the area moment of inertia (Iₓ) (2), the x-axis to bottom surface (t + d − yc) and the area moment of inertia (Iₓ) (3).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bending stress calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Inner depth (di)=((inner width (bi) ^ -exp b) × (-I denom × area moment of inertia (Iₓ) − (depth (d) ^ exp d) × mult × (width (b) ^ exp b) + PI × (depth (d) ^ exp d) × mult × (width (b) ^ exp b) + (depth (d) ^ exp d) × (width (b) ^ exp b)) ÷ (-mult + PI × mult + 1), 1 ÷ exp d)
C denom=depth (d) ÷ distance to surface (yc)
Area moment of inertia (Iₓ)=section modulus (Sₓ) × distance to surface (yc)
Applied bending moment (M)=maximum bending stress (σₘₐₓ) × (area moment of inertia (Iₓ) ÷ distance to surface (yc))
Web thickness (tw)=(-2 × (depth (d) ^ 2) × flange thickness (t) × width (b) − 3 × depth (d) × (flange thickness (t) ^ 2) × width (b) − 2 × (flange thickness (t) ^ 3) × width (b) + 6 × area moment of inertia (Iₓ) + 2 × the square root of ((depth (d) ^ 4) × (flange thickness (t) ^ 2) × (width (b) ^ 2) + 3 × (depth (d) ^ 3) × (flange thickness (t) ^ 3) × (width (b) ^ 2) + 4 × (depth (d) ^ 2) × (flange thickness (t) ^ 4) × (width (b) ^ 2) − 3 × (depth (d) ^ 2) × flange thickness (t) × area moment of inertia (Iₓ) × width (b) + 3 × depth (d) × (flange thickness (t) ^ 5) × (width (b) ^ 2) − 9 × depth (d) × (flange thickness (t) ^ 2) × area moment of inertia (Iₓ) × width (b) + (flange thickness (t) ^ 6) × (width (b) ^ 2) − 6 × (flange thickness (t) ^ 3) × area moment of inertia (Iₓ) × width (b) + 9 × (area moment of inertia (Iₓ) ^ 2))) ÷ (depth (d) ^ 3)
X-axis to bottom surface (yc)=((1 ÷ 2) × (depth (d) ^ 2) × web thickness (tw) + depth (d) × flange thickness (t) × web thickness (tw) + (1 ÷ 2) × (flange thickness (t) ^ 2) × width (b)) ÷ (depth (d) × web thickness (tw) + flange thickness (t) × width (b))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Bending stress calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the distance to surface, the area moment of inertia (Iₓ) and the x-axis to bottom surface — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Bending stress calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns inner depth (di), derived from the distance to surface, the area moment of inertia (Iₓ) and the x-axis to bottom surface. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Bending stress calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the distance to surface, the area moment of inertia (Iₓ) and the x-axis to bottom surface, which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter depth (d) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Depth (d) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Width (b) = 0 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Bending stress calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
